newsitem.title: INDIA: India ruling front defers decision on oil prices.
newsitem.headline: India ruling front defers decision on oil prices.

text.p: Resistance by left-wing parties prevented India's ruling United Front from reaching a consensus on Sunday to raise prices of some oil products to plug a mushrooming oil-subsidy bill, front officials said.
"No consensus has been reached," front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told reporters after a more than two and half hour meeting of the decision-making Steering Committee of the governing coalition.
"I do not want to anticipate what the consensus would be," Reddy said, adding that the Steering Committee would meet again in 10 days' time to discuss oil subsidy and other issues.
He said the government was unlikely to take a decision on the issue until the next committee meeting.

Analysts said the need to tackle India's gaping oil-pool deficit had become a serious test for Prime Minister I.K. Gujral in forging a consensus among 15 parties ranging from communists to free traders.

Both Gujral and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram have said the government must soon decide how to repay money it owes to oil companies for selling petroleum products at prices at well below global levels.

Alliance officials said Sunday's meeting highlighted sharp differences between the left parties and other members in the front on ways to plug the deficit, which Reddy said was growing at 300 million rupees ($8.4 million) a day.
The outstanding amount, called the oil pool deficit, totaled 155 billion rupees at the end of March.
Left-wing parties in the United Front have opposed raising prices, instead favouring increasing crude oil production and cutting import duties on crude oil and petroleum products.

Reddy quoted Sitaram Yechury of the (Marxist) Communist Party of India as saying that any increase in prices of petroleum products could be highly inflationary and suggested a cut in customs and excise duties to tackle the problem to some extent.

"This will have the most adverse of consequences economically and politically," the party, which lends crucial support to the alliance from outside, said in a statement. "This is unacceptable since viable alternatives exist."

Indian newspapers said the government had tentatively decided to raise the prices of diesel and kerosene with a plan that would trim about $1.5 billion from the subsidy bill. But the plan would spare petrol users.
Reddy said Chidambaram told the meeting the large oil pool account deficit was "absolutely unsustainable in fiscal terms."

Junior Petroleum Minister T.R. Balu said 300 million rupees were being added to the deficit every day due to import of petroleum products and the deficit was expected to balloon to 245 billion rupees by March 31, 1998.
"The petroleum minister indicated that some hike is desirable. But I am merely interpreting," Reddy said.
Members of Gujral's centrist Janata Dal party said there was need to take a realistic view and a decision could not be postponed indefintely.
